sections.heading: Amateurism
sections.specBullet: Amateurism as a code of sporting ethics

items.meaning: Participation in sport purely for the love of it, with no financial gain, based on the idea of athleticism: physical endeavour combined with moral integrity. It developed as a code of sporting ethics among the upper and, later, middle classes during the Victorian era.

paragraphs: Elite sport was dominated by the upper and middle classes, who wrote the rules that formed the basis of many national governing bodies, the Football Association in 1863 among them. Amateurism was built around high moral values: fair play, sportsmanship, and immediate acceptance of the rules and of referee decisions. Training was frowned upon, because it suggested professionalism.

Traces remain in modern British sport. Fair play and sportsmanship are still promoted through football's Fair Play Awards and pre-match and post-match handshakes, and Rugby Union, which retained amateurism until late in the twentieth century, still refers to the referee as Sir.

sections.heading: The Olympic oath
sections.specBullet: The Olympic oath and its relevance today

items.meaning: Written by Baron de Coubertin and first taken at the 1920 Antwerp Games. It is sworn at each Games' opening ceremony by one athlete, one judge committing to impartiality, and one coach, promising to compete respecting the rules, without doping, in the true spirit of sportsmanship.

rows: Evidence
The Olympics is still seen as a festival of fair play

Repeated doping scandals, including the Russian athletes banned from Rio 2016, and win-at-all-costs behaviour such as Philip Hindes admitting he deliberately crashed at London 2012 to trigger a restart

sections.heading: Sportsmanship
sections.specBullet: Sportsmanship and how it is encouraged

items.meaning: Conforming to the written rules, spirit and etiquette of a sport, showing fairness, self-control and respect for opponents and officials. Footballers kicking the ball out for an injured opponent, or cricketers walking before being given out, are examples.
Deceiving an official by over-acting, such as diving.

paragraphs: Sportsmanship is under pressure as winning becomes more important. Simulation is common, and so are breakdowns in etiquette, such as Suarez and Evra refusing to shake hands in 2012.

It can be encouraged through NGB campaigns such as the FA's Respect initiative, fair play awards such as UEFA's Fair Play Award, technology allowing correct decisions and the citing of missed offences, rule changes, on-field punishment such as sin-binning and sending off, post-event punishment, and rigorous drug testing.

sections.heading: Gamesmanship and the win ethic
sections.specBullet: Gamesmanship and the win ethic

items.meaning: The art of winning by cunning means without technically breaking the rules: stretching rules to their limit and disregarding etiquette, by delaying a restart, time-wasting, verbal sledging, or deliberately deceiving an official.
A win-at-all-costs mentality in which coming second is not acceptable. Sometimes called the Lombardian ethic, after Vince Lombardi.

paragraphs: The 1981 underarm bowling incident is the famous example of gamesmanship. Australia's captain Greg Chappell instructed his brother Trevor to bowl the last ball underarm, making it impossible for New Zealand to win. It was legal at the time, and hugely controversial.

The win ethic produces more serious examples: rugby coaches faking injury with blood capsules to bring on a specialist kicker, and Diego Maradona's Hand of God at the 1986 World Cup. It shows up across elite sport in formats with no drawn games, managers being sacked after poor results, higher levels of deviant behaviour, and media coverage that praises winners while criticising losers.

items.wrong: Gamesmanship is just another word for cheating.
items.right: Gamesmanship stays inside the written rules while ignoring their spirit. Breaking the rules outright is deviance.

sections.heading: Positive and negative deviance
sections.specBullet: Positive and negative deviance in relation to the performer

items.meaning: Behaviour that goes against the accepted norms of society. In sport it takes both positive and negative forms.

Over-adherence or over-conformity to sporting norms, such as training or competing while injured out of excessive commitment. Paula Radcliffe competing injured at the 2004 Athens Olympics is a well-known example.

Under-conformity to norms, often driven by the pressure to win: taking illegal performance-enhancing drugs, deliberately fouling or harming an opponent, accepting a bribe to fix a match, or diving to win a penalty.

items: Positive deviance is too much conformity, not good behaviour
Negative deviance is too little conformity
Both are deviance, because both depart from the accepted norm

sections.heading: Causes of performer violence
sections.specBullet: The causes of violence in sport among performers

items.meaning: Physical acts committed to harm others, seen in sports such as American football, rugby, football and ice hockey.

paragraphs: The win ethic helps explain why performers turn aggressive and eventually violent, especially when a result carries high emotional intensity, as in a local derby or a Cup Final.

Build-up in the media can leave a player over-psyched before the game starts, which is how Ben Flower came to be sent off in the 2014 Rugby League Grand Final. A decision that feels unjust does the same thing, with frustration at the officials tipping over into violence. So does being goaded, whether by an opponent or by the crowd: Zinedine Zidane's head-butt on Marco Materazzi in the 2006 World Cup Final followed exactly that.

items: Causes: the win ethic and high rewards, and the importance of the event
The nature of the sport, and NGBs being too lenient with punishments
Excitement and over-arousal, and refereeing decisions causing frustration

sections.heading: Preventing performer violence
sections.specBullet: Strategies to prevent violence among performers

items.meaning: Video technology used in rugby. Using more officials, or technology such as a fourth official or the TMO, reduces frustration caused by poor decision-making and removes perceived injustice.

paragraphs: NGB strategies include supporting officials' decisions with video replay and clearer rules, training officials to defuse situations, and punishing violence missed during the match using post-match video evidence, as in rugby league's on-report system.
Beyond that: promoting performers with good disciplinary records as role models, imposing harsh punishments such as bans or fines, and running education campaigns or fair play awards.

sections.heading: Causes of spectator violence
sections.specBullet: Football hooliganism and its causes

items.meaning: Unruly, violent and destructive behaviour.
The specific form of hooliganism carried out by over-zealous football supporters.

rows: Emotional
The heightened importance of certain fixtures, team loyalty taken to extremes, pre-match media hype, and violent behaviour on the pitch being mirrored by the crowd
Situational and social

Excessive alcohol and drug-taking, poor policing and crowd control, a key factor in the 1989 Hillsborough disaster, diminished individual responsibility within a large crowd, and organised gang violence
Other
Religious or sectarian discord, as between Celtic and Rangers, taunting between rival fans, and violence used as a display of masculinity

sections.heading: Combating football hooliganism
sections.specBullet: Strategies to combat football hooliganism

paragraphs: The main measures are banning or restricting alcohol sales, greater use of police intelligence, and tougher deterrents such as match bans, fines or imprisonment. After the 1985 Heysel Stadium disaster, UEFA banned all English clubs from European competition for five years, and Liverpool for six.

Grounds themselves were reshaped: CCTV installed around them, terraces replaced by all-seater stadiums, and segregation keeping rival supporters apart. Away from the ground, the press was pushed towards more responsible build-up coverage, kick-off times were set around what the police needed, and going onto the pitch was made an offence.

sections.heading: Implications of hooliganism for the sport
sections.specBullet: The negative implications of football hooliganism

paragraphs: Media coverage of fan violence damaged football's public image, which discouraged both participation and attendance. Anti-hooliganism measures such as travel bans unfairly affected law-abiding fans, and clubs could be excluded from competitions because of their fans' behaviour, as Liverpool were for six years after Heysel.
Hooliganism also drove up costs, through increased spending on security and policing, and images of English hooliganism abroad damaged England's reputation and its future bids to host major events.

sections.heading: Why performers dope
sections.specBullet: Social and psychological reasons for doping

items.meaning: The use of banned performance-enhancing substances by competitors in sport.

rows: Social, meaning the performer's environment

The win-at-all-costs mentality; the scale of extrinsic rewards on offer; pressure from coaches, family and media; weak deterrents and confidence that detection can be avoided; and poor role models in certain sports normalising doping
Psychological, meaning the mental effect chased

Beta-blockers to settle nerves where fine motor control decides the outcome, as in snooker; anabolic steroids to raise aggression for heavy-contact sports such as rugby; stimulants to counter a loss of self-belief and boost confidence at events such as the Olympics

items.wrong: Physiological and psychological reasons are interchangeable.
items.right: Physiological reasons concern the body's function. Psychological reasons concern the mind.

sections.heading: Physiological effects of drugs
sections.specBullet: The physiological effects of performance-enhancing drugs

rows: Anabolic steroids
Artificially manufactured hormones, such as THG, that assist protein storage and stimulate muscle growth, producing greater strength, power and leaner body composition
Power athletes, particularly sprinters
Liver, heart and immune system damage, acne, and aggression and mood swings
Beta-blockers
Calm the performer by blocking adrenaline, steadying nerves and improving accuracy
High-precision sports: archery, snooker, golf
Tiredness from lowered blood pressure, and reduced aerobic capacity
EPO (erythropoietin)
A naturally occurring hormone, also made artificially, that raises haemoglobin levels and oxygen-carrying capacity, improving endurance and delaying fatigue
Endurance performers
Blood clotting, stroke and, rarely, death

paragraphs: Lance Armstrong's stripped Tour de France titles and the BALCO scandal involving THG are the two best-known cases.

sections.heading: Implications of drug taking
sections.specBullet: The implications of doping for the sport and for the performer

paragraphs: For the sport, doping damages reputation and public interest, linking whole sports firmly to individual cheats: Justin Gatlin with athletics, Lance Armstrong with cycling, and the 2007 Tour de Farce. Suspicion then clouds the achievements of clean athletes such as Chris Froome and Mo Farah, and doping supplies negative role models to developing athletes.

rows: What doping means
Performance genuinely improves, and undetected users can gain fame and fortune

Serious health risks, with steroids linked to high blood pressure and EPO to heart disease and stroke; reputational damage and social isolation; lost income and sponsorship; legal consequences such as bans, stripped medals or imprisonment, as with Marion Jones; and accidental use is still punished, as when Alain Baxter lost his Olympic medal after an unknowing positive test

sections.heading: Eliminating performance-enhancing drugs
sections.specBullet: Strategies and organisations working to eliminate doping

items.meaning: Protects UK sport from doping across more than 40 sports.
The international foundation, established in 1999, that promotes, co-ordinates and monitors the global fight against drugs in sport.
One of the stricter procedures used, alongside out-of-competition testing.
Testing performers away from events, so doping cannot simply be timed around competition.
Requires athletes to make their location known so they can be tested.

items: Build a drug-free culture through education, such as UKAD's 100% Me programme, with organisations working together
Make punishments harsher and invest in testing technology
Name and shame negative role models, and make guilty performers lose funding and sponsorship

paragraphs: Positive role models such as Sir Chris Hoy are also used to promote clean sport.

sections.heading: Ongoing problems in the fight against doping
sections.specBullet: The difficulties in eliminating doping

items.meaning: Substances developed to hide the presence of banned drugs. New ones are continually developed.

paragraphs: Testers struggle to gain immediate access to athletes training overseas. New drugs and masking agents keep appearing, drugs can be taken accidentally, and regulations and testing procedures differ between countries and between sports, which makes a unified approach hard to achieve.

sections.heading: Should drugs be legalised?
sections.specBullet: Arguments for and against legalising drugs in sport

rows: The case

The battle against doping is expensive and time-consuming; drugs are easy to access and hard to eliminate; detection is not always effective; defining a drug against a legal supplement is difficult; drugs are sometimes taken accidentally; it is a matter of personal choice; and if everyone doped it would level the playing field

Serious health risks; negative role models for young people; a negative image for particular sports; increased pressure to dope; sporting success should rest on hard work and natural talent; drugs confer an unfair, immoral advantage and are cheating; only wealthier countries could afford them; and it is illegal

sections.heading: Why sport and the law now overlap
sections.specBullet: The relationship between sport and the law

items.meaning: The laws, regulations and judicial decisions governing sport and its athletes.
Behaviour departing from accepted norms. A rise in deviant acts in sport is one reason law and sport, historically separate, now overlap.

paragraphs: The other driver is rising professionalism and commercialisation, which forces sport to adhere to legal standards. Four groups are relevant: performers, officials, coaches and spectators.

sections.heading: The performer: injury and loss of earnings
sections.specBullet: Legislation and the performer: injury and loss of earnings

items.meaning: What a performer can bring for injury and loss of earnings.
Income lost as a result of an injury, which can be claimed for alongside the injury itself.
Compensation awarded. It requires proof of actual injury from an opponent's deliberate, harmful or reckless actions.
The critical test of whether an act is actionable. A foul may be acceptable in football, but a stamp or a punch would not be.

paragraphs: Injuries are usually accepted as an expected side-effect of sport, but a deliberate act to injure another can be illegal. Most player-violence issues are handled internally by NGBs, though some lead to prosecution, as with Duncan Ferguson in Scotland in 1995 and James Cotterill in England in 2006. Matt Holmes is the standard example of a footballer successfully claiming damages for a career-ending tackle.

sections.heading: The performer: contracts
sections.specBullet: Legislation and the performer: contracts and employment rights

items.meaning: What performers are. They are entitled to standard employment rights.
Gave EU footballers the right to move freely to another club at the end of their contract, without a transfer fee.

items: Performers need legal help over spectators attacking them, and opponents being too violent
Contractual issues with sponsors, and with employers
Equality of opportunity issues, and refereeing negligence

sections.heading: Officials: negligence
sections.specBullet: Legislation and officials: negligence and duty of care

items.meaning: Conduct falling below a reasonable person standard, which breaches the duty of care and results in foreseeable harm.
What officials owe participants: the elimination of dangers so the contest takes place in a safe environment.

rows: Smoldon v Whitworth and Nolan
The claim succeeded
The referee failed to follow guidelines on collapsed scrums
Allport v Wilbraham
The claim failed
The court preferred the defendant's evidence that the referee had adequately controlled the scrum

sections.heading: Coaches: duty of care
sections.specBullet: Legislation and coaches: duty of care

items.meaning: Requires a coach to take reasonable measures to keep participants safe.
Liability arises only where the risk was foreseeable but nothing was done about it.
Part of demonstrating reasonable care with children, alongside up-to-date contact and medical details, appropriate supervision ratios, first aid provision, and risk assessments.
In the place of a parent. The position a coach acts in where children are involved.

paragraphs: Coaches are responsible for health and safety, including first aid access and emergency contacts, for protection from abuse, both emotional and physical, and for educating athletes about drugs and supplements.

sections.heading: Spectators: safety and hooliganism
sections.specBullet: Legislation and spectators

items.meaning: The report into Hillsborough, and the key reference point for tackling hooliganism.

paragraphs: Spectators risk prosecution under the Public Order Acts for pitch invasion or racist chants. The measures used are all-seater stadia, control of alcohol sales, police-specified kick-off times, increased security and intelligence gathering, and tougher deterrents such as banning orders, fines and imprisonment.

sections.heading: Timeline of crowd safety legislation
sections.specBullet: The development of crowd safety legislation

rows: Occupiers' Liability Act (1957)
The occupier of a premises owes a common duty of care to visitors
Safety of Sports Grounds Act (1975)
Protects all spectators, covering all grounds in all sports
Sporting Events (Control of Alcohol etc.) Act (1985)
Banned alcohol possession at, or travelling to, a football match
Fire Safety and Safety of Place of Sport Act (1987)
Requires a fire safety certificate and sets maximum spectator numbers
Football Spectators Act (1989)
Allows banning orders on individuals who have committed offences
Football Offences Act (1991)
Created offences of throwing missiles, racist chanting, and pitch trespass

sections.heading: The golden triangle
sections.specBullet: Commercialisation, sponsorship and the golden triangle

items.meaning: The treating of sport as a commodity, with the market driving decisions.
The provision of funds or support in return for a commercial return.

The relationship between sport, commercialisation and the media, where each point depends on and profits from the other two. The media uses sport to attract audiences to sell to advertisers, businesses use the media to advertise and pay sport directly, and sport needs media exposure to attract sponsorship.

rows: Commercialisation brings
Increased income and promotion, increased sponsorship, better organised and funded events, and improved facilities

Sensationalised reporting; media and sponsors dictating kick-off times and changing the nature of a sport; minority sports losing out; excessive demands on performers; and pressure to win or to maintain lucrative contracts

sections.heading: Media coverage and ring-fencing
sections.specBullet: The media's influence on sport and the ring-fencing of events

items.meaning: Events that must be available on free-to-air television.
Events that must have live free-to-air coverage, such as the FA Cup Final and the World Cup Finals.
Events that can be pay-per-view provided a highlights package is free-to-air, such as Test cricket and the Open Golf.

paragraphs: Television is the best medium for sport, because it transmits live images to huge audiences instantly. Satellite television such as Sky Sports and BT Sport charges subscribers for access, as BT's purchase of Setanta showed.

The list of ring-fenced events has shrunk, because satellite channels offer riches sporting authorities cannot ignore. England home Test cricket moved from Category A to Category B from 2006. The arguments for continuing to ring-fence are reaching the widest range of viewers, avoiding restricting coverage to those who can pay, increasing geographical access, and protecting sporting heritage such as the Olympics and Wimbledon.

sections.heading: The growth of media money
sections.specBullet: The growth in the value of television rights

paragraphs: Premier League television rights income has grown enormously across successive deals since the early 1990s.

What broadcasters want is fairly consistent: a high level of skill, something that looks good on screen, rules simple enough to follow without explanation, a format that fits a short slot, and recognisable personalities to build the coverage around. Sports without those qualities, badminton and table tennis among them, get less airtime, which brings less commercial interest, which keeps them closer to amateur, which in turn keeps the airtime away. It is a vicious circle.

rows: For sport

Increases the profile of a sport and its performers; increases participation; creates more media-friendly variations of a sport such as Twenty20 cricket; generates higher income and commercial opportunities; and drives up standards of performance and behaviour

NGBs and performers lose control to television companies and sponsors; media control locations, kick-off times and playing seasons; too much sport on television can lead to boredom; inequalities of coverage disadvantage minority sports; and over-sensationalised coverage can encourage a win-at-all-costs attitude

sections.heading: Why sport attracts business
sections.specBullet: The attraction of sport to business, and marketability

paragraphs: Sport is attractive to business because it offers extensive media coverage, large audiences, a professional high-profile image, and advertising, merchandising and sponsorship opportunities. Sponsorship benefits companies through increased sales and brand awareness, improved company image, corporate hospitality opportunities, and tax deductions.

Not all elite performers are equally marketable. Sponsors want performers who present a positive image and are at the top of their profession. Nike's decision to back the world number one golfer Rory McIlroy, rather than his compatriot Graeme McDowell, rested on his continued success, his clean-cut image, and golf's high socio-economic audience.

sections.heading: Sponsorship and the elite performer
sections.specBullet: The effects of sponsorship on the elite performer

rows: For the performer

Increased wages, prize money and extrinsic rewards; increased availability of full-time professional contracts; a higher public profile requiring appropriate behaviour; and increased funding for training support and equipment

Increased pressure to win and win-at-all-costs behaviour; deviant behaviour such as playing while injured or taking drugs; being treated as a commodity with overly demanding sponsors; and inequality of funding for minority sports

sections.heading: The ethics of sport sponsorship
sections.specBullet: The ethical considerations of accepting sponsorship

paragraphs: An elite performer such as the boxer Anthony Joshua has to consider the nature of a sponsor, because performers are role models with a social duty to others, and has to weigh how much control a sponsor will have.

items: Weigh the social duty to others, whether personal appearances are demanded too much, and whether the product is opposed to the performer's reputation
There may be a negative impact on future sponsorship, and support is image dependent
The product may be opposed to the true nature of sport, and the performer is a role model for others

paragraphs: The opposite case is arguable too. Where a product is lawful, a performer is entitled to sign. Expecting them to take a stand puts their income on the line for a principle nobody else is being asked to fund. And being treated as a role model is something done to them, not something they volunteered for.

sections.heading: Effects on the sport as a whole
sections.specBullet: The positive and negative effects of commercialisation on a sport

paragraphs: Commercialisation acts on the sport itself as well as on the people in it. The gains are mostly financial, and the costs are mostly about control, because money arriving from outside a sport tends to come with expectations about how that sport is run.

rows: For the sport itself

Funding pays for facilities, equipment, coaching and talent identification, and for the technology that helps officials reach correct decisions. More events and competitions are staged, more role models become visible to draw people into the sport, and spectator involvement grows through team kit and merchandise

A sport can become over-reliant on commercial income, and is left exposed if that funding is withdrawn. Traditional supporters often resist the new competitions, rule changes and altered formats that broadcasters and sponsors ask for

sections.heading: Impact on coaches, officials and spectators
sections.specBullet: The impact of commercialisation on coaches, officials and spectators

rows: Coaches and managers
Higher profile and salaries, and increased funding for squads and facilities
Intense pressure to win, media demands, and inequalities between clubs
Officials
Higher profile and salary, and access to training and technology
Increased pressure to get decisions right, media scrutiny, and the risk of demotion if a faulty decision is highlighted
Spectators
Higher performance standards, improved facilities, and viewing technology such as Hawkeye
Increased costs, loss of traditional match features, more breaks in play, fewer tickets as more go to corporate hospitality, and less coverage of minority sports

items: Officials face over-dependency on technology, and faulty decisions being highlighted
Increased media pressure, and constant analysis of decisions
And a lack of technology at lower levels

sections.heading: Sports analytics and data collection
sections.specBullet: Research, sports analytics and types of data

items.meaning: A systematic process of investigation carried out to advance knowledge.

The study of data from sports performances using analytical tools to improve results. Opta's statistical analysis in cricket and football, and GPS analysis showing distances and speeds covered by rugby and football players, are examples.
Factual, numerical information gathered through formal, objective research, such as a VO2 max test.
Deals in words and is subjective, concerning feelings and opinions, such as coaches judging a gymnastics routine. It can be less precise and more time-consuming to collect.
Fact-based, measurable and observable, such as performance analysis at the EIS.
Rests on personal opinion, and is less measurable and meaningful, such as a parent's half-time comments.

sections.heading: Validity and reliability
sections.specBullet: The validity and reliability of data

items.meaning: The degree to which data actually measures what it claims to measure, and whether the conclusions drawn from it are appropriate.
Data being consistent, producing similar results when repeated. Threats include researchers misusing equipment such as skinfold calipers, or poorly maintained equipment.

paragraphs: Validity is a prerequisite for reliability. If data is not valid, its reliability is questionable.

sections.heading: Video and analysis programmes
sections.specBullet: Video motion analysis and performance analysis

items.meaning: Obtains information about moving objects from video, typically using a high-speed camera and computer software for frame-by-frame playback, to correct technique or ball release angle.
Records movement patterns, strategy and tactics.
Analyses the sporting impact of body movements through the quantitative study of motion, displacement, velocity and speed.
Provides objective feedback to a performer. Athletes and coaches recall only a fraction of a performance correctly, so performance analysis supplies what memory misses.
Allows users to view, edit and analyse video of technique.
Tags player actions in football using high-definition cameras.

sections.heading: Indirect calorimetry and the metabolic cart
sections.specBullet: Testing and recording equipment

items.meaning: Measures the heat or energy eliminated or stored in a system.
Measures oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide production, translating them into a heat equivalent. It is non-invasive and relatively accurate.
The equipment used for indirect calorimetry.
What the metabolic cart produces: the energy required by the body over 24 hours at rest. It varies with weight, age, gender and body chemistry, and smoking raises it.

paragraphs: It is used to determine energy requirements, to calculate nutritional needs, and to support obese individuals.

items: Sources of error: leakage of air, and overfeeding or underfeeding based on results
Single snapshots being less reliable than longer studies
Errors in measurement or recording

sections.heading: GPS and motion tracking
sections.specBullet: GPS and motion-tracking software and hardware

items.meaning: A space-based navigation system providing location and time information, tracking speed, distance and direction. In contact sports it can measure impact in G forces.

paragraphs: GPS supports objective decisions on substitutions, gauges fatigue to reduce injury risk, and manages workload for players returning from injury.

sections.heading: Maintaining data integrity
sections.specBullet: Data integrity

items.meaning: Maintaining the accuracy and consistency of data across its lifetime.

rows: Human error
Designing interfaces that prevent invalid input
Transmission errors
Using error detection and correction software
Software bugs or viruses
Controlling access
Hardware malfunction
Regular backups

sections.heading: Functions of sports analytics
sections.specBullet: The functions of sports analytics

items.meaning: At recreational level, monitoring heart rate or calories. At elite level, monitoring distance, pace, sleep and heart rate via smart wearable devices.
Video programmes such as Dartfish, and electrostimulation devices.
Real-time data on iPads and GPS receivers measuring distance and acceleration, helping coaches with tactics and substitutions. The quality of the information matters more than the quantity.
Qualitative scouting reports, and pathway analytics.
Benchmarking performance pathways, as in Tall and Talented, for sports requiring height such as basketball and rowing.

sections.heading: Adapted equipment
sections.specBullet: Adapted equipment for the elderly and for people with disabilities

paragraphs: Assistive and adapted technology is increasing, from specially designed wheelchairs and throwing frames in athletics to cross-country sit skis.

rows: Lightweight frames
Tennis and basketball
Reinforced frames
Contact sports such as rugby
Bucket seats and T-frames
Racing chairs

items.meaning: Devices such as the Springlite, which assists running through improved gait efficiency.

paragraphs: Adapted equipment for the elderly includes finger extension exercisers, low-impact pedal machines, and exercise balance beams.

sections.heading: Facilities
sections.specBullet: The development of facilities and the Olympic legacy

items.meaning: A Sport England initiative raising participation by providing community sports facilities.
The strand of Places People Play funding strategic, high-quality, multi-sport projects.

Sand and rubber infilled synthetic pitches suited to hockey, football and rugby, supporting frequent use and consistent conditions. They have been criticised as too rigid for joints and ligaments, though newer 3G and 4G surfaces have improved this, as at Widnes Vikings and Saracens, who play on artificial turf.
Provide multi-sport opportunities where dedicated single-sport surfaces are too expensive.
A specialist Olympic legacy facility.

sections.heading: The impact of technology
sections.specBullet: The impact of technology on sport, performers, coaches and the audience

items.meaning: Small improvements delivered by technology, such as Sir Dave Brailsford's heated trousers for British Cycling.
Where too much data reduces creative, instant reactions.

rows: Sport generally
Technology delivers marginal gains, increases participation and inclusivity through adapted equipment, and improves playing surfaces and player development data

Data can mislead without context; cost creates inequality between wealthy and less well-funded teams, as with Team Sky's technology partnership with Jaguar; paralysis by analysis; and a placebo effect with unproven equipment
Performers
Improved clothing such as the Speedo LZR Racer, plus better equipment, protective gear and recovery methods
Injury and over-aggression, cheating via masking agents, and expense creating inequality
Coaches
Video analysis through Dartfish and Prozone enables detailed opponent and player analysis
Over-reliance on data, and hacking risks
The audience
Statistics and mic'd up officials increase engagement and excitement, as does Hawkeye
Officiating technology can cause a loss of respect for officials, cost-driven inconsistency, and disruptive breaks in play
